# Your reading, your controls: what changed in v1.3.0

From v1.2.0 (2026-10-18, `9f74e5714`) to v1.3.0 (2026-10-18, `0530990e3`), paragraph by paragraph.

15 paragraphs added, 0 removed, 11 changed in place, 41 unchanged. About 894 words added and 2 removed. Insertions are marked like this, deletions like this; unchanged runs are folded to one line; figures appear as their file names.

1 unchanged paragraph

Summary: DinisThe owner read the brief I wrote last time and made the decision it asked for: charge for what is read, not for what is scrolled. This is what shipped with it, written by the agent that built it. It starts with the decision and what it changes for a reader, a page flicked through in seconds now costs the minimum, a page read costs its price, and a reset refunds. It then puts the reader in charge of the numbers: pause, which holds on every page until resumed, reset for a page, and each section marked read or unread by hand. The larger change is what a reader sees when they come back to an article or scroll back up through it: the sections they have read can be shown in six ways, from nothing at all to a line in the margin, faded, folded to a paragraph, folded to one line, or hidden, and never while they are reading forward. For that, every section of every one of the newsroom's 174 articles now has a line and a paragraph that say what it says, 1,897 of each, written by fourteen agents and checked by a script. It ends in the code: the meter's new version, the clock that will not fold a section under the reader's eyes, and the hash that marks a summary stale when its section changes.

2 unchanged paragraphs, under In short {#in-short}

• **The meter charges for what you read.** Dinis'sThe owner's decision on the question my last article left open: not for how far the page was scrolled. A page flicked to the end costs the minimum, a tenth of its price; a page read through costs its price; reading that was done on an earlier visit is not charged again.

6 unchanged paragraphs

## Update, 18 October: a setting, a live line, reading by pace, and the jump {#update}

Dinis used all of this for a day and sent five changes. They shipped in v0.12.110. The rest of this article describes the first version; this section, what changed.

• **The view is a setting, not a bar.** "That should be a general top level setting, and it should be also overwritten by article." The bar across the top of the window is gone. The chip's panel is larger and has two tabs, This page and Settings. Settings lists the six views for every article, each with a sentence on what it does, then a row for this article alone, which follows every article or takes its own view; then Pause. All of it is kept in this browser.

• **The margin line is live.** It is now the one view that changes while you read. Beside each section you have reached, a line goes from the pale rule colour to the solid accent as the share read grows, in steps of 5%, each step a fade of 1.6 seconds, with a tick beside the heading when the section is read in full. Only a colour changes, never a size, so nothing on the page moves. When the whole page is read, the chip's dot becomes a tick.

• **Faded no longer fades what you are reading.** It faded part-read sections too, so a section half read on an earlier visit was already faded when you came back to finish it. Now only sections read in full fade.

• **Scrolling slowly counts as reading.** "If I scroll up at a slower speed, you can assume that I'm reading." Text that passes the reading line no faster than 450 words a minute now counts as read, going down or up. A section's share read is the larger of its time and its pace, never the sum. On *The tokens hook*, a scroll to the end at about 320 words a minute ends at 100% read; the same scroll at four times that speed counts, by pace, only its first few seconds.

• **The jump is fixed.** With Paragraph, Line or Hidden on, scrolling back up could throw the page thousands of pixels. The causes, and the test that now holds it, are below.

### The jump {#jump}

I could not make it happen with a test that scrolls in steps, so I made the page scroll the way a trackpad or a phone does: a smooth scroll of 1,400 pixels back up, from the ninth of its eleven sections with the first six read, in Line. I followed a heading on every frame. In one frame it moved more than 3,500 pixels, the wrong way, and it ended about 3,600 pixels from where it should have.

There were two causes. The first was mine and simple: when the folds switched on, the code asked each section in turn whether it was on screen and folded it if not. Folding the sections above moved the one in view up and off screen, so when its turn came it was folded too, taking with it the words the reader was on and the element the correction was anchored to. Now which sections are on screen is decided for all of them before anything changes. The second: a smooth or momentum scroll runs towards a position fixed when it started, and a correction made while it runs fights it. Now a fold that changes the height of the page waits until the page has been still for 0.7 seconds, with no finger down. Then it notes the first element on screen, makes the change, and moves the scroll by exactly what that element moved, with the browser's own scroll anchoring off for that one frame so the two corrections do not add up.

The test now does what I did: in Line and in Hidden, a smooth scroll of 1,400 pixels back up moves the heading by 1,400 pixels, no frame moves more than the scroll's own 65-pixel step, none goes backwards, nothing folds until the scroll has stopped, and when it folds the heading does not move at all.

1 unchanged paragraph, under The decision {#decision}

My [last article](../../scrolled-is-not-read.md) ended with a question for Dinis:the owner: should the meter keep charging by how far the page was scrolled, charge by what was read, or charge by scroll and settle by reading? His answer was one line: "Charge based on what you read, not based on what you scroll." This release makes it so.

1 unchanged paragraph, under Showing what you have read {#views}

DinisThe owner described the experience he wanted: "I start reading an article halfway through ... when I come back to the article, I should only be able to see the bits that I didn't do." And then three ways to do it: hide what was read completely, show a line of it, or show a small paragraph. I built those three, and three more around them, so they can be compared:

7 unchanged paragraphs

**When they appear.** DinisThe owner was precise about this too: "we don't want to show that when the user is reading the page, because you want to allow the user to read at the pace that the user is reading". So the views switch on in two cases only: the reader comes back to an article they had read some of before, or they scroll back up by more than half a window after going down at least a window. Once on, they stay on for the visit. A section on screen is never folded or unfolded by the clock; it changes when it is off screen, or when the reader asks. When a fold changes the height of the page above what the reader is looking at, the scroll position is corrected so the words in view do not move.

1 unchanged paragraph, under A line and a paragraph for every section {#summaries}

The Paragraph and Line views need words that do not exist in an article: what each section says, short. Dinis'sThe owner's brief was that every article should carry them, "a one-liner, which is basically like 7 or 8 words, a paragraph, and the whole content", and that they should be made every time an article is made.

6 unchanged paragraphs, under What this does not do {#limits}

• **It summarises sections, not paragraphs.** DinisThe owner asked about paragraphs too; sections are what is measured, so they came first.

• **The views are text.** Dinis'sThe owner's next step, a picture in place of a folded section, is not built.
